title: Vitamin K1 Prophylaxis in Neonates: A Critical Review of the Evidence Base, Documented Prophylaxis Failure, and a Novel Mechanistic Hypothesis Linking Supraphysiological Neonatal Vitamin K1 Administration to Impaired Ductal Arteriosus Closure via Matrix Gla Protein Activation
content: Background : Intramuscular (IM) vitamin K1 prophylaxis has been recommended for routine administration to newborns since 1961 and is widely applied in high-income countries. The randomised controlled trial (RCT) evidence base supporting this policy rests on two trials conducted in the 1960s using vitamin K3 (menadione) — a molecule subsequently withdrawn from clinical use — neither of which evaluated late vitamin K deficiency bleeding (VKDB), intracranial haemorrhage (ICH), or death as primary outcomes. WHO and major systematic reviews grade this evidence as moderate to low quality.                                                                         Methods : Narrative review and mechanistic hypothesis paper. All peer-reviewed surveillance studies, systematic reviews, RCTs, and case series reporting vitamin K prophylaxis outcomes were reviewed. Mechanistic literature on Matrix Gla Protein (MGP), BMP-2 signalling, and ductal arteriosus vascular biology was reviewed. All references were independently verified against PubMed/NCBI and DOI databases prior to inclusion.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Results: The number needed to treat (NNT) derived from the Sutherland 1967 RCT is 74 (95% CI 47–177) to prevent one moderate-to-severe case of classical VKDB. Derived NNT for late VKDB ICH is approximately 8,000–10,000; for death, 25,000–50,000. Multiple peer-reviewed surveillance studies document prophylaxis failure in otherwise-healthy breastfed infants. Japan's fifth national survey (Takahashi et al., Pediatr Int 2011; PMID 21518125) found 88.7% of late VKDB cases had received at least one vitamin K dose. A novel mechanistic hypothesis is presented: physiologically low neonatal vitamin K may serve a functional role in facilitating ductus arteriosus (DA) anatomical closure by maintaining MGP in its inactive state, allowing BMP-2-mediated smooth muscle cell remodelling to proceed. Supraphysiological K1 from IM injection may activate MGP prematurely, modulate BMP-2 signalling, and potentially impair intimal cushion formation — a mechanism that warrants experimental investigation.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Conclusions: The evidence base for universal IM vitamin K prophylaxis is of low methodological quality by WHO GRADE standards. An animal study measuring MGP activation and DA closure timing following IM K1 is proposed as the minimum necessary first step. A human RCT in low-risk term infants — as called for by Golding and Greenwood (Arch Dis Child 2008; PMC2539847) — with DA closure timing and MGP activation as co-primary biological endpoints alongside VKDB incidence, is scientifically warranted.
